text:
alex: Heads-up — I'm sketching a shift from a hard per-tenant token cap to a layered "soft credits + circuit" approach for spikes. Want quick tradeoff check.
maya: Can you summarise the model? quick bullets pls.
alex: Sure — idea TL;DR: per-route soft-credit buckets that refill slowly + shadow accounting for sudden bursts. If a tenant exceeds soft credits, we start graceful degradation: lower-priority routes get shed first, then route-level circuit opens and request is routed to a lower-cost model variant or queue with 503+Retry-After. Global hard cap remains as last line.
sam: Two immediate concerns: 1) fairness — how do we avoid a fat tenant owning warm GPU KV caches? 2) observability — need fine-grained tracing for when we demote to fallbacks.
alex: Good points. For caches we propose cache-locality tagging: KV entries are tagged by tenant and route; eviction prefers entries from tenants currently over soft credits. It's a heuristic but cheap.
jin: What's the refill curve? linear or exponential backoff for refill rate? important for interactive vs batch workloads.
alex: Thinking of an adaptive refill: baseline linear refill (credits/sec) plus momentum component based on recent steady-state usage so interactive sessions don't starve. We can tune per-customer profile.
maya: How would this interact with Dedicated customers? We can't silently demote them to cheaper variants.
alex: For Dedicated/Reserved capacity customers we expose a strict policy flag: ignore soft shedding for routes covered by their SLA. The system still records shadow signals for capacity planning but won't route them to fallback.
sam: Abuse detection: how do we differentiate legitimate spike (e.g., product release) vs abuse? We don't want to throttle a real customer launching a campaign.
jin: We should couple credits with an abuse score from our classifier — high-abuse tenants have accelerated credit decay and tighter circuit thresholds. Also temporary probation windows where we rate-limit rather than circuit-break.
alex: Exactly — credits are influenced by signals: historical burstiness, abuse_score, billing_tier, and explicit reservation. The circuit triggers are percentile-based (p99 over window) instead of absolute tokens to handle traffic shape.
maya: Operationally, how do we test without risking prod UX?
alex: Plan: canary the behavior shadowed first — no actual reroutes, but tag affected requests and simulate fallback impact in the console. Next, enable soft-shed for a small traffic slice (5%) with verbose tracing and auto-rollback if user-visible latency or error rate changes exceed thresholds.
infra-bot: deploy request queued: rfc/draft/soft-credit-circuit v0.1 -> reviewers: @maya @sam. CI checks: load-sim tests, eviction-safety, observability hooks.
sam: Observability wishlist: per-tenant credit level timeseries, eviction events, cache-hit delta when demoted, fallback latency distribution, and a weave of request-id -> routing-decision.
jin: Also add synthetic probes that exercise fallback routes to avoid cold-start regressions.
maya: Sounds reasonable. My main ask: include clear operator override (manual open/close circuits) and an incident playbook for unexpected wide regressions.
alex: Agreed. I'll draft an RFC that includes: design, token math, refill curves, interaction matrix with Dedicated/Private, canary plan, metrics list, and runbook. Wanted to surface tradeoffs now: complexity vs cost savings and improved long-tail stability. Thoughts?
sam: +1 for RFC. Also include a small simulator (python) in the repo so product/infra can model a big-tenant burst.
jin: +1. Add a section on KV-tag eviction safety and memory overhead estimates.
maya: I'll review once the draft lands. Please include a few concrete knobs we can expose in Console for customer support to adjust.
alex: Will do — aiming to open the RFC this afternoon. Action items: alex -> RFC draft + simulator; sam -> metrics spec; jin -> cache eviction mem model; maya -> runbook template.
alex: Thanks all :thumbsup:
